observations.quote: mettalls are of no use in Physick, at least in the civill life
observations.name: any who out of their simplicity
observations.voice: QUOTED: any who out of their simplicity
observations.note: A view the author reports in order to answer it: that metals are of no use in physick. He says it is said out of simplicity.

observations.quote: there is no agreement or likenesse especially of those perfect Mettalls with mans body
observations.name: any who out of their simplicity
observations.voice: QUOTED: any who out of their simplicity
observations.note: Second part of the reported view: the perfect metals have no likeness with man's body. Reported to be rejected.

observations.quote: created, though not for Mans food yet for his Physick
observations.note: The author holds that metals, fruit of the Elements like living things and vegetables, were created for man's physick, not his food.

observations.quote: man partaketh of those Three first
observations.note: A set is named as 'those Three first', of which man partakes; the paragraph does not list them at this place. Interpreted: the words that follow name Animall, Vegetable and Minerall seed.

observations.quote: the Animall, Vegetable and Minerall sperm or seed have but one rise or originall, and differ onely in Quality of Place and Receptacle
observations.note: The author's answer: the three kinds of seed have one origin and differ only by place and receptacle.

observations.quote: See Theophrast. his Manuel.
observations.name: Theophrast. his Manuel
observations.note: The margin note names Theophrast. and his Manuel beside the paragraph on metals in physick.

observations.quote: since Man hath Physick for his body from the world because he is a world, therefore all Mineralls are for Mans good
observations.note: The note gives the ground: man is a world and has his physick from the world, so all minerals are for his good. Whether these are the author's words or drawn from the writing named is not shown.

observations.quote: that which is contained in the Physicall body is applyed to his minerall
observations.note: The note speaks of man's 'minerall', as if man has a mineral part to which what is in the physical body is applied.

observations.quote: Animall, Vegetable, and Minerall principles are one and the same in all things, but have various Receptacles
observations.note: The three kinds of principle are one and the same in all things; only their receptacles differ.

observations.quote: which is the generall seed of all things or subject of the first matter
observations.note: The text says what the 'one most principall and generall principall kind' is: the general seed of all things, or subject of the first matter.

observations.quote: to be distributed into three principall kinds, Animall Vegetable, and Minerall
observations.what: three principall kinds, Animall Vegetable, and Minerall
observations.note: The one general kind is set out as divided into three named kinds.

observations.quote: from which Nature hath the nature of Quick-silver to create every other Compound
observations.note: From this general kind Nature has 'the nature of Quick-silver' to make every compound; Quick-silver is named here as a nature, not as one metal among others. The lines given do not explain further.

observations.quote: All things are from one Principle, and tendeth to one
observations.note: One principle as origin and end of all things.

observations.quote: In Orpheus his Night and Hippocrates his river Orcus all things are but One
observations.name: Orpheus; Hippocrates
observations.note: Two named figures are brought as holding the same: in Orpheus's Night and Hippocrates's river Orcus all things are one.

observations.quote: like Anaxagoras his Pamsperm
observations.name: Anaxagoras
observations.note: Anaxagoras's Pamsperm is set beside them as a like name for the one. The margin note N176 at this place is an unread gap of foreign script.

observations.quote: which Aristotle unjustly condemned
observations.note: The author judges Aristotle's condemnation of the Pamsperm unjust, and (after the note mark) 'because he did not well understand it'.

observations.quote: which Nature is the Specifick of every Creature
observations.note: The one Nature, 'the Essence and Matter of all things', is said to be the Specifick of every creature.

observations.quote: according to the agitation and operation of the Universall spirit
observations.note: The differences between bodies are laid to two things: the place and receptacle, and the working of the Universall spirit.

observations.quote: This is the set Order for the government of the sublunary Family
observations.what: the set Order for the government of the sublunary Family
observations.note: Named order of nourishment: minerals nourish vegetables, vegetables beasts, beasts men.

observations.quote: which could not be if the nature of one thing did not by affinity partake of the nature of another
observations.note: The order of feeding rests on affinity of natures, which share in the first kind from which all things proceed.

observations.quote: Thus also the Spirit of life is united through out the whole body of man, but is various according to parts of the body in which it is.
observations.note: The note sets a parallel in man's body: one Spirit of life, varied by the part it is in.

observations.quote: All things flow from one Fountaine, which after they have done their work and quitted the Stage of Vanity, are returned to their own places
observations.note: All things come from one fountain and return to their own places after their work, where the text says they have unchangeable rest.

observations.quote: That universall Spirit which liveth in and quickneth this whole Masse, which worketh all in all, and filleth the whole world
observations.note: The text says what the universall Spirit does: lives in and quickens the whole mass and fills the world; it is also called 'that Power of God', and then the text gives what others call it.

observations.quote: Agrippa calleth it the subject of all mirability, the Ens or Being that cannot be comprehended by sence
observations.name: Agrippa
observations.note: Agrippa's name for the universall Spirit, as the text gives it.

observations.quote: Avicen saith, it is the Soule of the world powred into all things, building on the authority of Plato, the Arabians and Caldeans
observations.name: Avicen
observations.note: Avicen's name for it, the Soul of the world; the text adds that he builds on the authority of Plato, the Arabians and Caldeans.

observations.quote: this we must hearken to without any superstition or Idolatrous worship, giving honour onely to One God
observations.note: The author limits how these sayings are to be received: without superstition or idolatry, honour to God alone.

observations.quote: Rom. 8.
observations.name: Rom. 8
observations.note: The margin note names Rom. 8 beside the paragraph on all things returning to rest and the universall Spirit.

observations.quote: See Paracelsus his Apocalyps of Herines.
observations.name: Paracelsus his Apocalyps of Herines
observations.note: The note points to Paracelsus's Apocalyps of Herines beside the same paragraph.

observations.quote: The Soule of the world is a kind of united life, filling, gathering and knitting together all things
observations.note: The note says what the Soul of the world is: a united life that fills and knits all things together. Words after this in the note have unread letters.

observations.quote: by infusing into them occult qualities which are commonly called the Fift Effences
observations.note: The Soul of the world makes things fruitful by putting occult qualities into them, said to be commonly called the Fift Effences (spelling as given).

observations.quote: is the invisible Fire or fiery vigour by which all things are
observations.note: Nature, called 'the Image of Go' (one letter unread), is said to be the invisible fire or fiery vigour by which all things are multiplied.

observations.quote: Nature many times makes it selfe merry with its magistery or mastership
observations.note: The note pairs 'magistery' with 'mastership' as one sense, and speaks of Nature making merry with it.

observations.quote: Nature, I say, is that medium which by an Harmonicall consent joyneth the lowest things to the highest
observations.note: The author says in his own person what Nature is: the medium that joins lowest to highest. Other accounts of Nature stand at N178 and CH3.40.

observations.quote: sometimes is called Animall, sometimes Vegetable, sometimes Minerall, according to the diversity of the subject or receptacle
observations.note: The one Nature takes the three names from the subject or receptacle it is in.

observations.quote: the three Families of Nature
observations.note: The three kinds are named together as the three Families of Nature.

observations.quote: that Silesiac child in our age, which was born though not with a golden yet with a gilded tooth in the left and lower jaw, which I did both see and handle
observations.note: The author gives as an example of Nature's working a child born with a gilded tooth, which he says he saw and handled himself at Prague.

observations.quote: the Hermetick Phylosophy
observations.note: A named philosophy; to those who seek it the example is said not to be strange.

observations.quote: it is not unlawfull to pry into those things which exceed even naturall order
observations.note: The author holds that inquiry into things beyond natural order is lawful.

observations.quote: these are not so much astonyed at the sports of Nature
observations.note: The gilded tooth and the like are named 'sports of Nature'.

observations.quote: from the intimacy of more hid and secret Phylosophy
observations.note: A more hidden and secret philosophy is named as the source of what these seekers know.

observations.quote: that same Spirit and minerall Nature which produceth Gold in the bowells of the Earth is also in Man
observations.note: The spirit and mineral nature that makes gold in the earth is said to be also in man.

observations.quote: That Spirit in Gold is the same with the generating spirit of all Creatures, and is the same and onely generative Nature diffused through all things
observations.note: The spirit in gold is identified with the one generating spirit of all creatures.

observations.quote: This Spirit now hath assumed a Naturall body
observations.note: The spirit is said to have taken a natural body; the lines given do not say which body.

observations.quote: It is that which first moveth and ruleth Nature in all naturall things, it preserveth all things
observations.note: This spirit is said to be the first mover and ruler of Nature and the preserver of all things.

observations.quote: Albertus Magnus writeth, that in his time there hath been Gold found in the bodyes and heads of some that were hanged
observations.name: Albertus Magnus
observations.note: A report given to Albertus Magnus: gold found in the bodies and heads of the hanged.

observations.quote: There is not, saith he, that thing Elementated of the four Elements in which Gold Naturally may not be found in the last subtiliation thereof
observations.name: Albertus Magnus
observations.note: Words given to Albertus from 'his Book of Mineralls': gold may be found in every thing made of the four elements, at its last subtiliation.

observations.quote: the Phylosophers say that the matter of their Mystery may be had every where, because it consisteth in every Elementated thing
observations.name: the Phylosophers
observations.note: A saying given to 'the Phylosophers': the matter of their Mystery is to be had everywhere, because it is in every elementated thing.

observations.quote: Albertus also proveth, that the greatest Minerall vertue is in every Man, but especially in the head among the teeth
observations.name: Albertus
observations.note: Given to Albertus: the greatest mineral virtue is in every man, chiefly among the teeth; he reports gold grains found among the teeth of the long buried.

observations.quote: which could not be if there were not a minerall vertue in Man, which minerall vertue is in the Elixer of Phylosophers
observations.note: The mineral virtue in man is tied to the one in the Elixer of Phylosophers. The sentence does not show whether this conclusion is Albertus's or the author's.

observations.quote: In his Mineralls.
observations.name: Albertus
observations.note: The margin note names the writing of Albertus that the passage draws on.

observations.quote: Morienes that excellent Phylosopher, the most skilfull and expert Chymiologer
observations.note: The text introduces Morienes with the name 'Chymiologer'.

observations.quote: King Calid who inquired after the matter of the Elixer
observations.note: The matter of the Elixer is the thing asked after.

observations.quote: It is of thee O King, said he
observations.name: Morienes
observations.note: Morienes's answer to King Calid on the matter of the Elixer: it is of the king himself.

observations.quote: and thou are in its Mine
observations.name: Morienes
observations.note: The rest of Morienes's answer, after the note mark: the king is in the mine of the matter. 'Mine' is used of a man.

observations.quote: he saith that he got his matter out of a mean and worthlesse thing
observations.name: Raymund Lully
observations.note: Given to Raymund Lully: his matter came out of a mean and worthless thing. The thing is not named.

observations.quote: Wherein he never a jot differed from Raymund Lully that fearcher into this Magistery
observations.note: The author holds that Morienes and Lully say the same; the work is here called 'this Magistery'.

observations.quote: Lullius was a divine & most compleat Phylosopher, whom Paracel. blamed without a cause.
observations.note: The note praises Lullius and says Paracel. blamed him without cause.

observations.quote: The matter of a stone is said to be in every thing in respect of the first
observations.note: The note says in what respect the saying 'in every thing' is meant: in respect of the first mover in natural things (one letter of that word is unread).

observations.quote: which is calld the Vegetall Spirit, by whom our matter of a stone goeth beyond the rest
observations.note: The first mover in natural things is named the Vegetall Spirit; by it 'our matter of a stone' is said to go beyond the rest. The note adds that this spirit is in animals and vegetables as well as minerals.

observations.quote: Remember that Man is the most noble Creature of all, in whom there is the Naturall Mercuriality of the four Elements
observations.name: Riplaeus à Portis
observations.note: Given to Riplaeus à Portis, whom the author says agrees with both: in man is the natural Mercuriality of the four elements.

observations.quote: which is of little worth, and may be got out of its Mine by art
observations.name: Riplaeus à Portis
observations.note: Still Riplaeus's words: this thing is of little worth and can be got out of its mine by art. No step is given.

observations.quote: in every thing there is every thing potentially, though it doth not actually appear
observations.name: Rhasis
observations.note: Given to Rhasis, 'In his Book of Divinity': every thing is in every thing potentially, unseen. The author says Rhasis does not altogether dissent from Riplaeus.

observations.quote: I forbear to cite more Authors, though I might produce a great heap of Phylosophers, who confirme these things
observations.note: The author stops citing and claims many more philosophers confirm the same.

observations.quote: not by common and outside arguments, but by solyd reasons drawn from the inside of things
observations.note: Reasons drawn from the inside of things are set against common, outside arguments.

observations.quote: But these things are by the by.
observations.note: The author marks the run of authorities as an aside from his main matter.

observations.quote: The Chymicall way of Subtiliating Extracting, and Separating being imperfect, was not much used in Galens dayes
observations.note: The chymical way is named by three operations; the author says it was imperfect and little used in Galen's days, and altogether unknown to Galen.

observations.quote: for they knew not how to separate the bark and husk from the kernell
observations.note: The ancients' lack is put as not separating bark and husk from kernel; the section heading uses 'bark and rind' of the true physick.

observations.quote: he tryed all wayes and means to distinguish the facultyes of simple medicines, and discern the hot parts of vineger from the cold
observations.name: Galen
observations.note: Galen's own words as reported: he tried every way to tell apart the faculties of simple medicines and the hot and cold parts of vinegar.

observations.quote: to separate the contrary parts of vineger as well as of milk
observations.note: The step Galen is said to have sought a device for: separating the contrary parts of vinegar, as of milk. No method is given.

observations.quote: who in this thing might have obtained his desire if he had been well skild in the Distillatory Art
observations.note: The author holds that the Distillatory Art would have given Galen what he sought.

observations.quote: Nor is it any disgrace to Hippocrates or Galen that they knew not these things
observations.note: The author does not blame Hippocrates or Galen for not knowing these things.

observations.quote: which is the order and series of Gods works, and obey the power, word and command of God
observations.note: In a parenthesis Nature is said to be the order and series of God's works, borrowing all its virtue from him. Other accounts of Nature stand at CH3.32 and N178.

observations.quote: they doe not bestow upon mankind all things together and at once, but doe communicate particular gifts to severall ages
observations.note: God and Nature give particular gifts to particular ages and persons, not all at once; so the ancients' ignorance is no disgrace.

observations.quote: Doubtlesse if Galen had lived when Paracelsus did, he would not have envyed, but reverenced his learning
observations.note: The author's claim that Galen would have revered Paracelsus's learning and not been ashamed of his coals; the sentence goes on to say Galen would have served 'Theophraestus'. Interpreted: the sentence uses both names for one man.

observations.quote: to separate the three first (qualities) in vineger
observations.note: The three first of vinegar are named as things to separate; a bracketed word glosses them as 'qualities'. N181 speaks of 'the three first things' of milk and CH3.28 of 'those Three first'.

observations.quote: to learn the preparations of those high Magisteryes and Elixirs
observations.note: The preparations of magisteries and elixirs are named as the chief thing to learn.

observations.quote: neither would he have refufed to blow the coals or temper his stuffe, or watch his work
observations.note: Three tasks of the work are named: blowing the coals, tempering the stuff, watching the work.

observations.quote: who have not learned so much as their A. B. C. in the Spagyrick Physick
observations.note: The author's charge against the 'Colerick and Melancolick Philerastian Physitians'.

observations.quote: the Creation and composition of the internall Astrall Man, much lesse of the Mechanick Spirits of diseases
observations.what: the internall Astrall Man; the Mechanick Spirits of diseases
observations.note: Two things are named as matters these physicians know nothing of; the lines given do not explain them.

observations.quote: whom these men fear not to call a circumforaneous or rambling rayler, one that was no Phylosopher at all
observations.name: Philerastian Physitians
observations.note: What the opposing physicians call Paracelsus; reported to be rejected.

observations.quote: that never sufficiently commended Paracelsus, a thousand-fold more worthy then his adversaries, and the immortall glory of Germany
observations.note: The author's praise of Paracelsus over his adversaries.

observations.quote: who had the absolute knowledge of all Divine and Humane sciences, beyond what will be believed of him
observations.note: The author claims for Paracelsus absolute knowledge of all divine and human sciences.

observations.quote: with viperous hatred they accuse his course of life, aggravating his humane fraylties
observations.note: The author grants Paracelsus human frailties and says his accusers make them heavier.

observations.quote: We have all our faylings, happy is he that hath least
observations.note: The author answers the attacks on Paracelsus's life with the failings common to all.

observations.quote: Lib. 1. cap. 19.
observations.name: Galen
observations.note: The margin note gives book and chapter beside Galen's reported words; it does not name the work.

observations.quote: Whey, Butter and Cheese are the three first things of milk, for all Terresterity is Salt.
observations.note: The note says what the three first things of milk are, and adds that all 'Terresterity' is Salt.

observations.quote: I wish the ambitious Physitians of that time, who robbed others of their due praise, who cast a Serpents eye upon Theophrastus
observations.note: The author blames the physicians of that time for envy toward Theophrastus. Interpreted: the text uses the names Theophrastus and Paracelsus for the same man.

observations.quote: who is the End of all Humane actions and Physick, viz. that we should love the Best and Greatest God, and all our neighbours as our selves
observations.note: The giver of the command is called the End of all human actions and of Physick, and the command is stated.

observations.quote: his human imperfections which none will excuse, they should have born with the like tendernes of compassion where with they pardon Galens impiety who scoffed at the doctrin of Moses & Christ
observations.note: None will excuse Paracelsus's imperfections, but they deserved the forbearance given to Galen's impiety; the author charges Galen with scoffing at Moses and Christ.

observations.quote: Doubtles he would have more clearly have manifested to thankful posterity his Secrets which God disclosed to him, and written more plainly and perfectly of Preparations
observations.note: Theophrastus is said not to have set out his Secrets clearly nor written plainly of Preparations, and this is laid to the ill treatment he had.

observations.quote: by being againe put to seek out the certainty and truth of that which Theophrastus discoursed and writ of, and to long for the true Preparations in the practicall proceeding
observations.note: The present Spagyrick Profession must seek out again the truth of what Theophrastus wrote and lacks the true Preparations in practice.

observations.quote: that there are so few to be found who have the true medicines prepared according to Theophrastus his minde, of which he treateth at large in his Books
observations.note: Few have the true medicines prepared as Theophrastus meant, though his books treat of them at large.

observations.quote: for they require solutions, mortifications, cohibitions, resuscitations, &c. truly Phylosophycall, which cannot be understood without true Physick
observations.note: The workings the true medicines require are named, without what is done to what; the list is left open with '&c.'. They cannot be understood without true Physick and (after the note mark) Astronomy and Chymistry.

observations.quote: truly Phylosophycall
observations.note: The named workings are qualified as 'truly Phylosophycall', which sets them apart from a plain sense of the same words; the lines given do not say how.

observations.quote: nor are they compleated in a short time, but with much tediousnesse to Phylosophists who are impatient of delay
observations.note: The preparations take long; those impatient of delay are called 'Phylosophists'.

observations.quote: In his second Book of the difference of Pulses.
observations.name: Galen
observations.note: The margin note names the writing of Galen beside the charge that he scoffed at the doctrine of Moses and Christ.

observations.quote: See Paracelsus in Paragr.
observations.name: Paracelsus in Paragr.
observations.note: The margin note points to Paracelsus 'in Paragr.' beside the statement that few have the true medicines.

observations.quote: A Physitian must be an Astronomer, otherwise Paracelsus saith that his Physick is but imposture and a cheat.
observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.note: The note gives Paracelsus's saying that a physician's physick without astronomy is imposture.

observations.quote: Therefore many with Icarus are drowned in a great Sea.
observations.note: A figure: those who fail are drowned like Icarus; the note does not say it plainly.

observations.quote: But truly I think this wicked generation is not worthy of such medicines.
observations.note: The author's judgement that his generation is not worthy of the true medicines.

observations.quote: his mighty and marvellous works from unworthy Men
observations.note: God is said to withhold his mighty works from unworthy men for the world's sins and ingratitude; a word of foreign script before these is unread.

observations.quote: He will never suffer those Secrets to be known, especially in these corrupt and perilous times
observations.note: God will never let those Secrets be known, above all in these times.

observations.quote: almost all men have a burning desire after making Gold
observations.note: Nearly all desire gold-making and (after the note mark) neglect the due preparation of their medicines.

observations.quote: the onely cause thereof is their not knowing the Metaphysicks of Paracelsus, the true Phylosophy
observations.note: The cause given: they do not know the Metaphysicks of Paracelsus, called the true Phylosophy.

observations.quote: those large Books which Theophrastus directeth unto in his Labyrinth of Physitians
observations.name: Theophrastus in his Labyrinth of Physitians
observations.note: A writing of Theophrastus, his Labyrinth of Physitians, is named as directing to large books to be read first, before any preparation is begun.

observations.quote: before they set upon the preparations, separations and resolution of Naturall things
observations.note: The steps of the work, to come only after that reading.

observations.quote: There are four Pillars of Physick, Phylosophy, Alchymistry, Astronomy, and the Physicall vertue or medicine.
observations.note: The note numbers and names four Pillars of Physick.

observations.quote: most Chymists betake themselves to Court, and are turned from the truth by the glitter of Court-service
observations.note: Most Chymists go to court and are turned from the truth there.

observations.quote: for many years I have taken notice that many have begun well, but deluded with these toyes, have made an ill end
observations.note: The author gives this as his own observation over many years.

observations.quote: this Divine Spagyrie, the most wonderfull and approved Art
observations.note: The art is named and praised as divine and approved; said to be disparaged by the ruder sort.

observations.quote: though for many ages suspected of greatest uncertainty, and most abominable deceit
observations.note: The author grants the art has long been suspected of uncertainty and deceit, and says it is cast aside even by those who intend the same business.

observations.quote: What is said of, or spoken against abuse, imposture, and wicked arts, is not that for which things otherwise good may or ought to be condemned
observations.note: Abuse of a thing is no ground to condemn the thing; the better the thing, the more destructive its abuse.

observations.quote: the Athenian Thrasos who will have Light to be Darkenesse, and Darkenesse to be Light
observations.name: the Athenian Thrasos
observations.note: Opponents named by a figure, 'the Athenian Thrasos', whose view is reported to be rejected; the lines given do not say who is meant.

observations.quote: For the world seeketh not the Truth but its own Honour
observations.note: The author's charge against the world that defends them.

observations.quote: we our selves should be the cause of the imminent destruction of our own Kingdome
observations.note: God gives 'us' up to hate one another and so to cause a near destruction of 'our own Kingdome'.

observations.quote: O fountaine of Truth and Wisedome, consider our condition
observations.note: The author turns to prayer at the close of the text given.

observations.quote: that God would stirr up the minds of some which may bring to light the Truth that is in sciences and Faculties
observations.note: He hopes God will before long move some to bring to light the truth in the sciences.

observations.quote: for as yet the Invention of Arts hath not attained the utmost end
observations.note: The finding out of arts is not yet complete.

observations.quote: confute the delusions and errours of the schoolmen not with words, but deeds; not Syllogistically, but Really and indeed
observations.note: The schoolmen are to be refuted by deeds, not by words or syllogisms.

observations.quote: the time of Revocation and Regeneration drawing nigh
observations.what: the time of Revocation and Regeneration
observations.note: A coming time is named, at which 'every imperfect thing will of necessity come to nought'.

observations.quote: where Titles, Degrees and glistering Names make men proud, their is no humility, no life of Christ, no holy Spirit
observations.note: Pride in titles and degrees is set against humility, the life of Christ and the holy Spirit.

observations.quote: who suffer the Old man to be ruled by the Sydereall Spirit
observations.note: Pride of titles is tied to the Old man ruled by the Sydereall Spirit in most; the lines given do not explain either name.

observations.quote: graciously deliver them from the chaines of Utter Darknesse and incessant janglings of Putatitious and conceited Schollers
observations.note: The closing prayer for the lovers of Truth, against the wrangling of 'Putatitious' and conceited scholars.

dropped.reason: repeats A43/B45, which carry the matter of their Mystery and the term
'our matter of a stone' is carried by the Vegetall Spirit observation (A53, B57) and B56
the text does not set the two places against each other: blaming Lullius without cause is not said to bear on Paracelsus's knowledge
the text does not show that the Truth hoped for in CH3.46 is 'those Secrets'; no conflict borne out

voices.voice: QUOTED: any who out of their simplicity
voices.quote: mettalls are of no use in Physick
voices.basis: 'If there be any who out of their simplicity shall say': a view reported in order to answer it

voices.quote: Minerals conduce much to the health of Man
voices.basis: follows 'See Theophrast. his Manuel.'; the note does not show whether these are Croll's words or drawn from that writing

voices.quote: In Orpheus his Night and Hippocrates his river Orcus
voices.basis: the oneness of all things is set in their named figures

voices.quote: like Anaxagoras his Pamsperm
voices.basis: the Pamsperm is given to Anaxagoras by name

voices.quote: Agrippa calleth it
voices.basis: name and verb of saying 'calleth'

voices.quote: Avicen saith, it is the Soule of the world
voices.basis: name and verb of saying 'saith'

voices.quote: The Soule of the world is a kind of united life
voices.basis: follows 'See Paracelsus his Apocalyps of Herines.'; the note does not show whether these are Croll's words or drawn from that writing

voices.quote: Albertus Magnus writeth
voices.basis: name and verbs 'writeth', 'saith he', from 'his Book of Mineralls'

voices.quote: the Phylosophers say
voices.basis: group named with verb 'say'

voices.quote: Albertus also proveth
voices.basis: name, verbs 'proveth' and 'writeth', and N179 'In his Mineralls.'

voices.quote: which could not be if there were not a minerall vertue in Man
voices.basis: the sentence does not show whether this conclusion is Albertus's or Croll's

voices.quote: It is of thee O King, said he
voices.basis: Morienes named, 'said he'; continues after the note mark 'and thou are in its Mine'

voices.quote: he got his matter out of a mean and worthlesse thing
voices.basis: 'when he saith', of Raymund Lully

voices.quote: Remember that Man is the most noble Creature of all
voices.basis: 'Riplaeus à Portis agreeth with them both:' followed by his words

voices.quote: You may easily, saith he, perceive
voices.basis: Rhasis named, 'In his Book of Divinity', 'saith he'

voices.quote: he tryed all wayes and means
voices.basis: 'as may be gathered from his own words, when he saith'; N181 gives book and chapter

voices.quote: a circumforaneous or rambling rayler
voices.basis: 'whom these men fear not to call': words reported in order to reject them

voices.quote: Whey, Butter and Cheese are the three first things of milk
voices.basis: follows the pointer 'Lib. 1. cap. 19.'; the note does not show whether these are Croll's words or drawn from that book

voices.quote: A Physitian must be an Astronomer
voices.basis: 'Paracelsus saith'

voices.quote: who will have Light to be Darkenesse
voices.basis: view given to 'the Athenian Thrasos' in order to reject it
